dz.syn: cap pneumonia chest infection lrti curb-65 curb65 lower respiratory tract infection
dz.s: Severity (CURB-65 with clinical judgement) decides the antibiotic. Treat for 5 days, then review.
dx: Chest X-ray; CURB-65 (CRB-65 in the community)
Moderate–high severity: blood and sputum cultures, pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens
Respiratory viral PCR in season
dz.rx: Low severity: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS orally. Moderate: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS (add clarithromycin 500 mg BD if atypical infection suspected). High: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS IV (or 500/125 mg TDS orally) plus clarithromycin 500 mg BD.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg OD, or clarithromycin 500 mg BD (low–moderate severity); levofloxacin 500 mg BD (high severity, consider its safety warnings).
dz.dur: 5 days, then stop if clinically stable.
dz.ipc: Pneumococcal vaccine (PPV23) at 65 y and in risk groups; influenza vaccination; smoking cessation.
notes: High severity in hospital: consider a corticosteroid (IV hydrocortisone first) for 4–7 days or until discharge (NICE NG250).
Higher doses (amoxicillin up to 1 g TDS) are often used in hospital; follow local policy.
dz.cause: S. pneumoniae commonest; H. influenzae (COPD), Mycoplasma (epidemic young adults), Legionella, Chlamydophila psittaci (birds), S. aureus after influenza.
dz.clin: Cough, fever, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea; consolidation on examination. Mycoplasma: cold agglutinins, haemolysis, erythema multiforme.
dz.pearl: PVL S. aureus: necrotising pneumonia with haemoptysis and leucopenia — add clindamycin or linezolid to suppress toxin.
trial: Hydrocortisone within 24 h reduced 28-day mortality in severe CAP on ICU (excluding influenza and septic shock).

dz.syn: hap hospital acquired pneumonia nosocomial pneumonia vap ventilator
dz.s: Pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after admission. Choice depends on severity and the risk of resistant organisms.
dx: Chest X-ray, blood cultures, sputum (or endotracheal aspirate) culture
Check previous cultures for MRSA and resistant Gram-negatives
dz.rx: Not severe and low resistance risk: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS orally. Severe or higher risk (over 5 days in hospital, recent antibiotics, known colonisation): IV piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, meropenem or levofloxacin per local policy.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy (not severe): doxycycline, co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD or levofloxacin. Add vancomycin, teicoplanin or linezolid if MRSA is suspected or confirmed.
dz.ipc: VAP bundle: head-up 30–45°, daily sedation hold, subglottic suction, oral care with toothbrushing, early extubation.
dz.cause: Early onset (<5 days): community flora. Late onset: Enterobacterales, P. aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, S. aureus including MRSA.
dz.clin: New or progressive infiltrate with fever, purulent secretions and worsening oxygenation ≥48 h after admission or intubation.
dz.pearl: Ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis without infiltrate rarely needs treatment — avoid chasing colonisers.
trial: 8 days was non-inferior to 15 days for VAP, with more recurrence when non-fermenters such as P. aeruginosa were the cause.

dz.s: Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical) does not need antibiotics; aspiration pneumonia is treated like community- or hospital-acquired pneumonia.
dx: Chest X-ray (often right lower lobe)
Swallow assessment
dz.rx: Treat as community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia by severity and setting. Extra anaerobic cover is not routinely needed unless there is lung abscess or empyema.
notes: Antibiotics started for pneumonitis can often be stopped within 48 hours if the patient improves quickly.

dz.syn: copd aecopd exacerbation chronic obstructive bronchitis
dz.s: Give antibiotics only if the exacerbation is severe or sputum becomes purulent, balancing likely benefit against resistance.
dx: Sputum culture if previous treatment failed or frequent exacerbations
Chest X-ray if pneumonia possible
dz.rx: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS, doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg OD, or clarithromycin 500 mg BD.
dz.alt: Higher risk of treatment failure: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS, levofloxacin 500 mg OD or co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD. IV: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, clarithromycin, co-trimoxazole or piperacillin–tazobactam.

dz.s: Send sputum before starting, and use previous sputum results to choose.
dx: Sputum culture with every exacerbation
dz.rx: Without previous results: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS, or clarithromycin 500 mg BD, or doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg OD, if allergic. Pseudomonas colonisation: ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD (750 mg BD for severe).
dz.alt: IV if severe: piperacillin–tazobactam or ceftazidime by previous susceptibility.

dz.s: Antivirals for people in hospital or at risk of complications, started as soon as possible.
dx: Nose and throat swab for respiratory viral PCR
dz.rx: Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days (adjust for kidney function). Start in hospitalised patients even after 48 hours of symptoms.
dz.alt: Severe immunosuppression or suspected oseltamivir resistance: zanamivir (inhaled, or IV in severe illness via specialist advice).
dz.dur: 5 days (10 days often used if severely immunosuppressed).
dz.ipc: Droplet precautions in hospital; side room or cohort.
notes: Post-exposure prophylaxis for at-risk contacts: oseltamivir 75 mg OD for 10 days, when UKHSA says flu is circulating or in outbreaks.
dz.cause: Influenza A (H1N1, H3N2; avian H5N1, H7N9) and B; segmented RNA genome. Antigenic drift causes epidemics, shift causes pandemics.
dz.clin: Abrupt fever, myalgia, headache, dry cough; complications include primary viral and secondary bacterial pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalopathy.
dz.pearl: Post-influenza S. aureus pneumonia (often PVL) is rapidly fatal. Aspirin in children → Reye’s syndrome.
trial: Oseltamivir shortened time to symptom relief by about a day and reduced lower respiratory complications and admission.

dz.syn: covid covid-19 sars-cov-2 coronavirus paxlovid nirmatrelvir
dz.s: Treatment depends on whether the patient needs oxygen and their risk of severe disease.
dx: Respiratory viral PCR or lateral flow test
dz.rx: Needing oxygen: dexamethasone 6 mg OD for up to 10 days; consider tocilizumab or baricitinib per NICE. Not in hospital but at high risk: nirmatrelvir with ritonavir (check interactions) within 5 days of symptoms, or other options listed by NICE.
dz.dur: Dexamethasone up to 10 days; nirmatrelvir–ritonavir 5 days.
dz.ipc: Follow local respiratory infection precautions.
notes: Use the Liverpool COVID drug interaction checker before ritonavir-containing treatment.

dz.s: Paroxysmal cough with whoop or post-tussive vomiting. Notifiable; antibiotics mainly reduce spread.
dx: Cough under 2 weeks: nasopharyngeal PCR or culture
Cough over 2 weeks: serology (anti-pertussis toxin IgG) or oral fluid
dz.rx: Within 21 days of cough onset: clarithromycin 500 mg BD for 7 days or azithromycin 500 mg OD for 3 days.
dz.alt: Macrolide unsuitable: co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD for 7 days.
dz.ipc: Notifiable. Exclude from work or school until 48 hours of antibiotics, or 21 days from cough onset if untreated.
notes: Prophylaxis for close contacts in priority groups (infants, pregnant women, healthcare workers) follows UKHSA guidance.
dz.cause: Bordetella pertussis; pertussis toxin and filamentous haemagglutinin. Highly transmissible; waning immunity in adolescents and adults.
dz.clin: Catarrhal phase, then paroxysmal cough with whoop and post-tussive vomiting for weeks (‘100-day cough’); apnoea in infants.
dz.pearl: Infants under 3 months die of pulmonary hypertension and apnoea — leucocytosis >30 predicts severity.
trial: Vaccination in pregnancy was ~90% effective against pertussis in infants under 3 months in England.

dz.s: Severe pneumonia, often with confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and raised CK; ask about travel, hot tubs and cooling towers.
dx: Urinary antigen (detects serogroup 1 only)
Sputum or lower respiratory sample for Legionella PCR and culture (needed for public health typing)
dz.rx: Levofloxacin 500 mg BD (or OD for mild disease), or clarithromycin 500 mg BD.
dz.dur: 7–10 days; 14–21 days if severe or immunosuppressed.
dz.ipc: Notifiable (as Legionnaires’ disease). Not spread person to person.
dz.cause: Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 from aerosolised warm water (25–45 °C): cooling towers, showers, spa pools. Risk: smokers, older men, immunosuppressed.
dz.clin: Severe pneumonia with high fever, confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs and raised CK. Pontiac fever is a mild, self-limiting flu-like form.
dz.pearl: Ask about travel, hotels and hospital stays in the incubation period (2–10 days); clusters drive environmental sampling.
trial: Investigation of the American Legion convention outbreak identified Legionella and its water-borne aerosol spread.

dz.s: Drain the pleural space; antibiotics alone rarely clear it.
dx: Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration: pH under 7.2 or frank pus means a chest drain
Pleural fluid culture in blood culture bottles
dz.rx: Community-acquired: co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime plus metronidazole. Hospital-acquired: piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem per local policy.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: per local policy (for example clindamycin with ciprofloxacin).
dz.dur: Usually 2–6 weeks; guided by drainage and response.
notes: Intrapleural tPA with DNase if drainage fails (MIST-2).

dz.syn: sore throat pharyngitis tonsillitis strep throat feverpain centor quinsy
dz.s: Most are viral. Use FeverPAIN or Centor to decide; look for quinsy and other red flags.
dx: FeverPAIN 0–1 or Centor 0–2: no antibiotic
FeverPAIN 2–3: no antibiotic or back-up prescription
FeverPAIN 4–5 or Centor 3–4: immediate or back-up antibiotic
dz.rx: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg QDS (or 1 g BD).
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 250–500 mg BD for 5 days, or erythromycin.
dz.ipc: Scarlet fever is notifiable; exclude from school for 24 h after starting antibiotics. Outbreak control for iGAS in care homes.
dz.cause: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), spread by droplets; peak in school-age children, late winter and spring.
dz.clin: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absent cough. Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.
dz.pearl: Sequelae: rheumatic fever (prevented by treatment) and glomerulonephritis (not prevented). Avoid amoxicillin — EBV rash.
trial: Penicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis markedly reduced subsequent rheumatic fever — the basis for treating sore throat.

dz.s: Usually viral and settles within 2–3 weeks. Look for orbital or intracranial complications.
dx: Symptoms under 10 days: no antibiotic
10 days or more: consider high-dose nasal steroid, or a back-up antibiotic
dz.rx: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg QDS.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg OD, or clarithromycin 500 mg BD. Very unwell or high risk: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS.

dz.syn: malignant otitis externa necrotising otitis externa skull base osteomyelitis pseudomonas
dz.s: Severe ear pain out of proportion, often in older people with diabetes. Usually Pseudomonas; urgent ENT.
dx: CT and MRI of the temporal bone
Ear swab or biopsy culture before antibiotics
CRP and ESR to monitor
dz.rx: Anti-pseudomonal treatment per ENT and microbiology: for example IV ceftazidime or piperacillin–tazobactam, or oral ciprofloxacin if susceptible and mild.

dz.syn: cellulitis erysipelas skin infection ssti leg red
dz.s: Mark the edge, look for a portal of entry, and rule out necrotising infection, DVT and venous eczema.
dx: Blood cultures if systemically unwell
Swab only if there is an open wound or pus
dz.rx: Flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g QDS orally; IV flucloxacillin 1–2 g QDS if severe. Near the eyes or nose: co-amoxiclav.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 500 mg BD, erythromycin or doxycycline (200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg OD). Severe: cefuroxime, ceftriaxone or clindamycin. MRSA: vancomycin, teicoplanin or linezolid.
notes: Redness can spread for the first 24–48 hours even when treatment is working.

dz.syn: necrotising fasciitis nec fasc nf flesh eating fournier gangrene
dz.s: A surgical emergency: pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity. Do not wait for imaging if suspected.
dx: Urgent surgical review for debridement
Blood cultures, tissue cultures at surgery
LRINEC can support, but a low score does not rule it out
dz.rx: Broad IV cover per local policy, for example meropenem or piperacillin–tazobactam, plus clindamycin 1.2 g QDS (to switch off toxin; above the licensed dose, per local protocol). Add vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA risk.
dz.dur: Until no further debridement needed and clinically improving; review with microbiology.
dz.ipc: Invasive group A strep is notifiable: contacts may need prophylaxis.
notes: Consider IV immunoglobulin for streptococcal toxic shock.
dz.cause: Type I polymicrobial (diabetes, perineum — Fournier’s gangrene); type II group A strep ± S. aureus; Vibrio and Aeromonas after water exposure; clostridial gas gangrene.
dz.clin: Pain out of proportion to signs, rapid spread, tense oedema, bullae, crepitus, skin anaesthesia; septic shock.
dz.pearl: Clindamycin suppresses toxin synthesis and is unaffected by inoculum (Eagle) effect.
trial: IVIG did not improve physical function or mortality in necrotising soft-tissue infection.

dz.syn: bite dog bite cat bite human bite animal bite
dz.s: Clean and assess. Consider tetanus, rabies (animal bites abroad, any bat) and blood-borne viruses (human bites).
dx: Prophylaxis: human bite breaking skin with blood; cat bite breaking skin; dog or other bite with deep wound, high-risk site (hands, feet, face, genitals, joints) or at-risk patient
dz.rx: Co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg BD plus metronidazole 400 mg TDS.
dz.dur: Prophylaxis 3 days; treatment of infection 5 days.
notes: Human bites: assess hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV risk.

dz.syn: diabetic foot infection ulcer osteomyelitis dfi
dz.s: Grade the severity, probe to bone, and involve the diabetic foot team.
dx: Deep tissue sample (not a surface swab) after debridement
X-ray; MRI if osteomyelitis suspected
dz.rx: Mild: flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g QDS. Moderate or severe: flucloxacillin with or without gentamicin and/or metronidazole; co-amoxiclav with or without gentamicin; ceftriaxone with metronidazole; or piperacillin–tazobactam (severe).
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin, erythromycin or doxycycline (mild); co-trimoxazole with or without gentamicin and/or metronidazole (moderate–severe). Add vancomycin, teicoplanin or linezolid if MRSA.
dz.dur: Mild 7 days; moderate–severe 7 days minimum then review; osteomyelitis about 6 weeks.

dz.s: Golden crusted lesions; S. aureus or group A strep.
dz.rx: Localised, not bullous: hydrogen peroxide 1% cream BD–TDS (fusidic acid 2% TDS if unsuitable). Widespread, bullous or unwell: flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 250–500 mg BD.
dz.ipc: Exclude until lesions crusted and healed, or 48 hours after starting antibiotics.

dz.syn: pvl panton valentine leukocidin boils recurrent abscesses necrotising pneumonia
dz.s: Suspect with recurrent boils or abscesses, clusters in households or sports teams, or necrotising pneumonia.
dx: Send pus or swabs asking for PVL testing (reference laboratory)
dz.rx: Drain abscesses. Antibiotics by susceptibility if needed (for example flucloxacillin; doxycycline or clindamycin). Necrotising pneumonia: IV clindamycin and linezolid, with rifampicin; consider IV immunoglobulin.
dz.ipc: Decolonise the patient and household once lesions heal (for example nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine body wash for 5 days).

dz.syn: scabies sarcoptes itch mites crusted norwegian
dz.s: Intense itch worse at night, burrows in finger webs and wrists. Crusted scabies is very contagious.
dz.rx: Permethrin 5% cream to the whole body, repeated after 7 days. Treat all household and close contacts at the same time.
dz.alt: Malathion 0.5% liquid if permethrin unsuitable. Crusted scabies or outbreaks: oral ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg (specialist advice) with topical treatment.
dz.ipc: Contact precautions for crusted scabies; wash bedding and clothes at 50°C or above.

dz.syn: shingles herpes zoster vzv ophthalmicus ramsay hunt
dz.s: Antivirals within 72 hours of rash help most when over 50, immunocompromised, severe pain or rash, or ophthalmic involvement.
dx: Vesicle swab for VZV PCR if unsure
dz.rx: Aciclovir 800 mg five times a day, or valaciclovir 1 g TDS, or famciclovir 500 mg TDS. Disseminated or severely immunocompromised: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg TDS.
dz.ipc: Cover lesions. Airborne and contact precautions if disseminated or immunocompromised.
notes: Eye involvement (nose tip, eye symptoms): same-day ophthalmology.

dz.syn: septic arthritis joint infection hot joint
dz.s: A hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise. Aspirate before antibiotics unless septic.
dx: Joint aspirate: Gram stain, culture, crystals
Blood cultures
Gonococcal NAAT (urine and swabs) if sexually active
dz.rx: IV flucloxacillin 2 g QDS (add gentamicin if Gram-negative risk). Suspected gonococcal: ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours (BASHH 2025). MRSA risk: vancomycin.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clindamycin or vancomycin.
dz.dur: Usually 4–6 weeks in total, with early oral switch when improving.
dz.ipc: Aseptic technique for intra-articular injections; prompt orthopaedic review.
notes: Urgent orthopaedic washout. Prosthetic joints: see prosthetic joint infection.
dz.cause: S. aureus commonest; streptococci; N. gonorrhoeae if sexually active; Kingella kingae in children under 4; Gram-negatives in elderly and IVDU.
dz.clin: Acute hot, swollen, painful joint with restricted movement — usually knee; fever may be absent. Risk: RA, prosthetic joint, diabetes, steroids.
dz.pearl: Crystals do not exclude sepsis. Kingella is fastidious — PCR or blood culture bottle inoculation.
trial: After surgical drainage, 2 weeks of antibiotics was non-inferior to 4 weeks for native-joint septic arthritis.

dz.syn: prosthetic joint infection pji hip knee replacement arthroplasty
dz.s: Plan surgery and microbiology together; hold antibiotics until samples are taken unless septic.
dx: Joint aspirate (culture, cell count)
At surgery: at least 5 separate periprosthetic tissue samples
Blood cultures
dz.rx: After sampling: IV vancomycin plus broad Gram-negative cover (for example piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem) per local policy, then target to cultures.
dz.dur: Usually 6–12 weeks depending on the operation (DAIR or revision).
dz.ipc: Laminar flow theatres, skin preparation, cefuroxime or flucloxacillin + gentamicin prophylaxis at induction; MSSA decolonisation pre-op.
notes: Rifampicin is added for staphylococci when metalwork is retained, once bacteraemia has cleared and wounds are dry (never alone).
dz.cause: S. aureus; CoNS and Cutibacterium on implants; Salmonella in sickle cell; Pseudomonas after foot puncture through trainers; polymicrobial in diabetic foot.
dz.clin: Haematogenous in children (metaphysis) and adults (vertebral discitis); contiguous in diabetic foot; PJI early (<3 months), delayed or late.
dz.pearl: A sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis is diagnostic. Cutibacterium needs 14-day incubation.
trial: Oral antibiotics were non-inferior to IV during the first 6 weeks for bone and joint infection.

dz.syn: vertebral osteomyelitis discitis spondylodiscitis spinal infection epidural abscess
dz.s: Back pain with fever or raised CRP. Look for a source (endocarditis) and spinal cord compromise.
dx: MRI whole spine
Blood cultures (×2–3); CT-guided biopsy if cultures negative, ideally before antibiotics
Echo if S. aureus or streptococcal bacteraemia
Consider TB and Brucella
dz.rx: If stable, wait for microbiology. If septic or neurological signs: IV flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA risk) plus Gram-negative cover per local policy.
dz.dur: 6 weeks (non-inferior to 12 weeks in the Bernard 2015 trial for most cases).

dz.syn: meningitis bacterial meningitis meningococcal pneumococcal neck stiffness
dz.s: Give antibiotics within an hour; do not delay for lumbar puncture or CT.
dx: Blood cultures and meningococcal PCR
Lumbar puncture if safe (CSF cell count, protein, glucose, culture, PCR)
dz.rx: Ceftriaxone 2 g BD IV with dexamethasone 10 mg QDS (start with or before the first dose). Add amoxicillin 2 g every 4 hours if Listeria risk (over 60 or immunocompromised).
dz.alt: Severe penicillin or cephalosporin allergy: chloramphenicol (with co-trimoxazole for Listeria).
dz.dur: Meningococcal 5 days; pneumococcal 10–14 days; Listeria 21 days.
dz.ipc: Meningococcal: droplet precautions for 24 hours of treatment; notifiable; contacts need prophylaxis.
dz.cause: N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae in adults; GBS, E. coli and Listeria in neonates; Listeria if >60 y, pregnant or immunosuppressed.
dz.clin: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, confusion; non-blanching rash in meningococcal sepsis. Infants: bulging fontanelle, poor feeding.
dz.pearl: CT first only if focal signs, GCS ≤12 or papilloedema. Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria.
trial: Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose reduced death and unfavourable outcome, with the clearest benefit in pneumococcal meningitis.

dz.syn: encephalitis hsv encephalitis confusion fever seizures
dz.s: Fever with altered behaviour, seizures or focal signs. Start aciclovir immediately.
dx: MRI brain, lumbar puncture (HSV and VZV PCR), EEG
Send autoimmune antibodies if infection not found
dz.rx: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg TDS (adjust for kidney function).
dz.dur: HSV encephalitis 14–21 days (repeat LP before stopping).
dz.ipc: Notifiable (acute encephalitis).
dz.cause: HSV-1 in adults (reactivation or primary); HSV-2 in neonates and recurrent lymphocytic (Mollaret’s) meningitis.
dz.clin: Fever, altered behaviour, dysphasia, temporal lobe seizures; olfactory hallucinations. Mortality ~70% untreated.
dz.pearl: Start aciclovir empirically within 6 h of admission. Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis follows HSV in up to 1 in 4.
trial: Aciclovir roughly halved mortality compared with vidarabine and became standard therapy.

dz.syn: brain abscess cerebral abscess ring enhancing
dz.s: Headache, focal signs, fever often absent. Find the source: teeth, sinuses, ears, heart, lungs.
dx: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging
Neurosurgical aspiration for culture (before antibiotics if possible)
Blood cultures, echo, HIV test (toxoplasmosis)
dz.rx: Ceftriaxone 2 g BD IV plus metronidazole 500 mg TDS; add vancomycin or linezolid if post-neurosurgery or S. aureus suspected.
dz.dur: Usually 6–8 weeks; oral step-down possible after initial response (ESCMID 2024).
dz.ipc: Treat dental and sinus sepsis promptly; screen for right-to-left shunts.
dz.cause: S. anginosus group and anaerobes from sinus, dental or otogenic spread; S. aureus after trauma or surgery; Nocardia, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus if immunosuppressed.
dz.clin: Headache is the commonest symptom; fever in only half; focal deficit, seizures, raised intracranial pressure.
dz.pearl: LP is contraindicated — herniation risk. Look for HHT or cyanotic congenital heart disease.
trial: Mortality from brain abscess fell from ~40% to ~10% over five decades with CT/MRI, stereotactic aspiration and better antibiotics.

dz.s: Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics if stable; echo; modified Duke criteria; endocarditis team.
dx: Blood cultures ×3 from separate venepunctures
TTE then TOE
Duke–ISCVID criteria
dz.rx: Use the site’s endocarditis guide for empirical and organism-specific regimens.
dz.dur: Usually 4–6 weeks; partial oral treatment (POET) for selected patients.
dz.ipc: Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures no longer routine in UK (NICE); good oral hygiene in high-risk patients.
dz.cause: Viridans streptococci (native); S. aureus (acute, PWID, right-sided); CoNS (early prosthetic); enterococci (elderly, GU source); HACEK; Coxiella, Bartonella (culture-negative).
dz.clin: Fever with a new murmur; emboli (stroke, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions), immune phenomena (Osler’s nodes, Roth spots, GN).
dz.pearl: Surgery for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or large vegetation with emboli. S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy.
trial: Oral step-down after ≥10 days IV was non-inferior to full IV therapy in stable left-sided endocarditis.

dz.syn: sab staph aureus bacteraemia mssa mrsa bacteremia
dz.s: Never a contaminant. Repeat blood cultures, echo, remove lines, find the source, infection specialist review.
dx: Repeat blood cultures at 48–72 hours
Echo (TOE if high risk)
dz.rx: MSSA: flucloxacillin 2 g QDS IV or cefazolin 2 g TDS. MRSA: vancomycin (AUC-guided).
dz.dur: At least 14 days IV from the first negative culture if uncomplicated; 4–6 weeks if complicated.
dz.ipc: MRSA screening and decolonisation; line care bundles; mandatory surveillance; ID consultation for every case.
dz.cause: MSSA and MRSA from lines, skin and soft tissue, injecting drug use, surgical sites; 30-day mortality ~20–30%.
dz.clin: Fever, rigors; metastatic foci in spine, joints, psoas, valves and lungs. Persistent bacteraemia suggests an undrained focus or endocarditis.
dz.pearl: Never dismiss as a contaminant. Cefazolin is an alternative to flucloxacillin; vancomycin is inferior for MSSA.
trial: Adjunctive rifampicin did not improve outcome in S. aureus bacteraemia, though it reduced recurrence.

dz.syn: line infection crbsi clabsi central line picc hickman catheter related bloodstream
dz.s: Paired blood cultures from the line and a vein; remove short-term lines for S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida and mycobacteria.
dx: Paired cultures: line positive at least 2 hours before the peripheral set suggests the line
Look at the exit site and tunnel
dz.rx: Empirical: vancomycin (or teicoplanin), plus Gram-negative cover if septic, neutropenic or femoral line. Then target to cultures.
dz.dur: Coagulase-negative staph: 5–7 days after removal. S. aureus: at least 14 days. Candida: 14 days after the first negative culture.

dz.syn: gram negative bacteraemia e coli bacteraemia klebsiella bacteremia urosepsis
dz.s: Find and control the source; 7 days is enough for most once controlled.
dx: Repeat cultures only if not improving
Imaging of the likely source
dz.rx: Per source and local policy; then the narrowest active agent. ESBL: a carbapenem for serious infection.
dz.dur: 7 days for most uncomplicated cases (Yahav 2019, BALANCE 2024).

dz.s: Identify high-risk patients and give antibiotics within an hour, after blood cultures.
dx: Blood cultures before antibiotics, lactate
Look hard for a source and send relevant samples
dz.rx: Broad-spectrum per local policy (often piperacillin–tazobactam, with gentamicin in shock). Add MRSA cover if colonised.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: per local policy.
dz.dur: Review at 48–72 hours; narrow or stop.

dz.syn: c diff cdiff clostridium difficile cdi pseudomembranous colitis
dz.s: Stop unnecessary antibiotics and PPIs; assess severity; isolate.
dx: Stool GDH and toxin testing
WCC, creatinine and lactate for severity
dz.rx: First episode: vancomycin 125 mg QDS orally for 10 days. Recurrence or high risk of recurrence: fidaxomicin 200 mg BD for 10 days.
dz.ipc: Side room with enteric precautions; soap and water handwashing.
dz.cause: Toxigenic C. difficile (toxins A and B; binary toxin in ribotype 027) after clindamycin, cephalosporins, quinolones or co-amoxiclav; age and PPIs.
dz.clin: Diarrhoea ≥3 unformed stools in 24 h; colitis, ileus, toxic megacolon. Severe: WCC >15, creatinine >50% rise, temperature >38.5 °C, colitis on imaging.
dz.pearl: PCR+/toxin− suggests colonisation. Bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B) reduced recurrence but has been withdrawn.
trial: Duodenal FMT cured 81% of recurrent CDI vs 31% with vancomycin alone; the trial stopped early for benefit.

dz.s: Diagnostic tap in every patient with ascites admitted to hospital. Neutrophils over 250/mm³.
dx: Ascitic fluid cell count and culture in blood culture bottles
dz.rx: Per the site’s SBP guide and local policy (for example ceftriaxone, or piperacillin–tazobactam if hospital-acquired).
notes: IV albumin on day 1 and day 3 reduces kidney failure and death.

dz.syn: cholangitis ascending cholangitis biliary sepsis charcot
dz.s: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; biliary drainage is the key treatment.
dx: Blood cultures, LFTs, ultrasound or MRCP
Tokyo guidelines grade severity
dz.rx: Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS IV (mild–moderate), or piperacillin–tazobactam (severe or healthcare-associated) per local policy.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: per local policy (for example ciprofloxacin or a cephalosporin with metronidazole).

dz.syn: liver abscess pyogenic amoebic hepatic abscess klebsiella
dz.s: Pyogenic (biliary or bowel source; hypervirulent Klebsiella) or amoebic (travel).
dx: Ultrasound or CT; drain if large
Blood cultures, aspirate culture
Entamoeba serology if travel
dz.rx: Pyogenic: ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, or piperacillin–tazobactam. Amoebic: metronidazole 800 mg TDS for 7–10 days, then a luminal agent (paromomycin).
notes: Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae: check eyes (endophthalmitis) and look for other abscesses.

dz.syn: intra-abdominal infection peritonitis appendicitis perforation abscess
dz.s: Source control (surgery or drainage) matters most.
dx: CT abdomen
Cultures from pus at drainage
dz.rx: Co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime (or ceftriaxone) plus metronidazole; piperacillin–tazobactam if severe or healthcare-associated (local policy).
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: per local policy.
dz.dur: About 4 days after adequate source control (STOP-IT 2015).

dz.s: Uncomplicated and systemically well: no antibiotic, analgesia and review.
dx: CT if complications suspected
dz.rx: Systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or significant comorbidity: co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS. IV: co-amoxiclav, or cefuroxime plus metronidazole, or gentamicin plus metronidazole.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: cefalexin plus metronidazole, trimethoprim plus metronidazole, or ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole.

dz.syn: h pylori helicobacter dyspepsia peptic ulcer eradication
dz.s: Test with urea breath test or stool antigen (no PPI for 2 weeks before).
dz.rx: PPI BD plus amoxicillin 1 g BD plus clarithromycin 500 mg BD or metronidazole 400 mg BD.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: PPI plus clarithromycin 250–500 mg BD plus metronidazole 400 mg BD.
dz.dur: 7 days (NICE); many now use 14 days in line with Maastricht VI.
notes: Avoid clarithromycin or metronidazole if used for any reason in the past year.

dz.s: Notifiable (acute). Check everyone before chemotherapy or immunosuppression.
dx: HBsAg, anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe, HBV DNA, LFTs
Test for HIV, hepatitis C and D; vaccinate contacts
dz.rx: Refer to hepatology. Antivirals (tenofovir or entecavir) depend on phase, DNA level and liver disease.
dz.ipc: Notifiable (acute hepatitis).
notes: Before immunosuppression: HBsAg-positive needs prophylaxis; anti-HBc-positive may need prophylaxis or monitoring.
dz.cause: HBV, partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus with reverse transcriptase; vertical, sexual, blood-borne. High prevalence in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
dz.clin: Acute: often subclinical; jaundice in adults; fulminant failure <1%. Chronic: cirrhosis, HCC (even without cirrhosis), extrahepatic polyarteritis nodosa.
dz.pearl: Chronicity ~90% after perinatal vs <5% after adult infection. Reactivation with rituximab — prophylaxis if anti-HBc positive. HDV needs HBsAg.
trial: Universal infant HBV vaccination reduced childhood hepatocellular carcinoma — the first vaccine to prevent a cancer.

dz.s: Curable with 8–12 weeks of direct-acting antivirals.
dx: Anti-HCV, then HCV RNA (or core antigen) to confirm current infection
Test for HIV and hepatitis B
dz.rx: Refer to the hepatitis C service (operational delivery network). Pan-genotypic regimens: sofosbuvir–velpatasvir 12 weeks or glecaprevir–pibrentasvir 8 weeks.
dz.ipc: Notifiable (acute).
notes: Check drug interactions (Liverpool HEP checker).
dz.cause: HCV, positive-sense RNA flavivirus; genotypes 1–6. Injecting drug use, pre-1991 blood products, unsafe medical procedures abroad; low vertical and sexual risk.
dz.clin: Acute usually asymptomatic; ~75% chronic. Cirrhosis over decades, HCC; extrahepatic cryoglobulinaemia, membranoproliferative GN, porphyria cutanea tarda.
dz.pearl: Antibody persists after cure — test RNA for reinfection. HBV reactivation on DAAs: check HBsAg first. HCC surveillance continues if cirrhotic.
trial: Sofosbuvir–velpatasvir for 12 weeks achieved ~99% SVR12 across genotypes 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.

dz.s: Faecal–oral; notifiable. Contacts can be protected with vaccine.
dx: HAV IgM
dz.rx: Supportive. Watch for acute liver failure (INR).
dz.ipc: Notifiable. Exclude from work or school for 7 days after onset of jaundice or symptoms.
notes: Close contacts: hepatitis A vaccine within 14 days of exposure (immunoglobulin for some).

dz.s: UK infection is mostly genotype 3 from pork; usually self-limiting but can become chronic when immunosuppressed.
dx: HEV IgM and HEV RNA (PCR); PCR in immunosuppressed patients
dz.rx: Supportive. Chronic infection: reduce immunosuppression; ribavirin (specialist).
dz.ipc: Notifiable (acute hepatitis).

dz.s: Usually self-limiting; most need no antibiotic.
dx: Stool culture or PCR
dz.rx: Only if severe, prolonged or immunocompromised: azithromycin 500 mg OD for 3 days (or clarithromycin 500 mg BD for 5–7 days).
dz.alt: Avoid quinolones (high resistance).
dz.ipc: Notifiable as food poisoning. Food handlers and other risk groups: exclude until 48 hours free of symptoms.
dz.cause: C. jejuni (and C. coli) from undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk and untreated water; low infectious dose.
dz.clin: Prodromal fever and myalgia, then cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea; may mimic appendicitis or IBD.
dz.pearl: Commonest UK bacterial gastroenteritis. Guillain–Barré via molecular mimicry of gangliosides (GM1); reactive arthritis.
trial: About a quarter of Guillain–Barré cases had recent C. jejuni infection, linked to axonal damage and worse recovery.

dz.s: Usually no antibiotic. Treat if severe, very young or old, immunocompromised or bacteraemic.
dx: Stool culture; blood cultures if febrile
Bacteraemia in over-50s: look for endovascular infection
dz.rx: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD or IV ceftriaxone (or azithromycin) guided by susceptibility.
dz.dur: Gastroenteritis 5–7 days if treated; bacteraemia 10–14 days.
dz.ipc: Notifiable as food poisoning. Exclusion for risk groups until 48 hours free of symptoms.

dz.syn: typhoid enteric fever paratyphoid salmonella typhi xdr
dz.s: Fever after travel (especially South Asia). Constipation is as common as diarrhoea.
dx: Blood cultures (repeat), stool culture
Tell the laboratory: hazard group 3
dz.rx: Ceftriaxone 2 g OD IV empirically. Pakistan (XDR typhoid): meropenem, with or without azithromycin. Oral when susceptible: azithromycin 500 mg OD (1 g on day 1 in some protocols).
dz.ipc: Notifiable. Exclusion and clearance stool samples for risk groups (UKHSA).
dz.cause: Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi A, B, C; faecal–oral spread; humans only reservoir; most UK cases after travel to South Asia.
dz.clin: Step-ladder fever, headache, constipation then diarrhoea, relative bradycardia, rose spots, splenomegaly. Complications: perforation, bleeding in week 3.
dz.pearl: Chronic gallbladder carriage (‘Typhoid Mary’) — cholecystectomy may be needed. Laboratory-acquired infections reported.
trial: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (Vi-TT) gave ~82% efficacy in children aged 9 months to 16 years.

dz.s: Bloody diarrhoea; can be sexually acquired. Extensively drug-resistant strains are rising.
dx: Stool culture with susceptibility
Sexual health screen if sexually acquired
dz.rx: Treat if severe or immunocompromised, guided by susceptibility (for example ciprofloxacin or azithromycin).
dz.ipc: Notifiable (infectious bloody diarrhoea). Exclusion and clearance samples for risk groups.

dz.syn: stec e coli o157 vtec haemolytic uraemic syndrome hus bloody diarrhoea
dz.s: Bloody diarrhoea; risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome, especially in children.
dx: Stool PCR or culture
FBC, film, U&E daily if unwell (watch for HUS)
dz.rx: No antibiotics and no anti-motility drugs (both increase HUS risk). Supportive care.
dz.ipc: Notifiable (HUS too). Strict exclusion for risk groups until clearance samples negative.
dz.cause: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, mainly O157:H7; cattle reservoir, undercooked beef, raw vegetables, petting farms. Infectious dose <100 organisms.
dz.clin: Bloody diarrhoea, often without fever. HUS 5–10 days later in ~10% of children: haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, AKI.
dz.pearl: stx2 carries greater HUS risk. Antibiotics trigger phage induction and toxin release.
trial: Children given antibiotics for E. coli O157 had a much higher risk of HUS — the basis of the no-antibiotics rule.

dz.s: Prolonged watery diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss.
dx: Stool PCR or antigen
dz.rx: Metronidazole 400 mg TDS for 5 days (or 2 g OD for 3 days).
dz.alt: Tinidazole 2 g single dose.
dz.ipc: Exclude risk groups until 48 hours free of symptoms.

dz.syn: norovirus winter vomiting bug diarrhoea vomiting outbreak
dz.s: Sudden vomiting and diarrhoea; spreads quickly in wards and care homes.
dx: Stool PCR
dz.rx: Supportive (fluids).
dz.ipc: Enteric precautions until 48 hours free of symptoms; close bays in outbreaks; soap and water.

dz.syn: uti cystitis lower urinary tract infection dysuria
dz.s: Women under 65: diagnose on symptoms. Men, pregnancy and catheters: send urine culture.
dx: Urine culture for men, pregnancy, over 65s, treatment failure, recurrence
dz.rx: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg MR BD (if eGFR 45 or more), or trimethoprim 200 mg BD (if low resistance risk).
dz.alt: Second line: pivmecillinam 400 mg then 200 mg TDS, or fosfomycin 3 g single dose.
dz.dur: Women 3 days; men and pregnancy 7 days.
dz.ipc: Remove or change catheters; avoid catheter dipsticks; prophylaxis for recurrent UTI after review; cranberry evidence weak.
notes: Pregnancy: nitrofurantoin (avoid at term); amoxicillin or cefalexin by culture.
dz.cause: E. coli ~80%; Klebsiella, Proteus, enterococci; S. saprophyticus in young women; Pseudomonas with catheters and instrumentation.
dz.clin: Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain. Pyelonephritis: loin pain, fever, rigors, vomiting. Older adults present with delirium.
dz.pearl: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy and before urological surgery. Proteus: struvite stones, nitrofurantoin-resistant.
trial: Nitrofurantoin for 5 days gave better clinical resolution of cystitis than single-dose fosfomycin (70% vs 58%).

dz.syn: pyelonephritis upper uti kidney infection loin pain
dz.s: Send urine culture; blood cultures if systemically unwell.
dx: Urine culture
Imaging if obstruction or no response in 48–72 hours
dz.rx: Oral: cefalexin 500 mg BD–TDS (up to 1–1.5 g TDS–QDS), or ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD; co-amoxiclav or trimethoprim only if culture susceptible. IV: amoxicillin (if susceptible), co-amoxiclav, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin.
dz.dur: Cefalexin or co-amoxiclav 7–10 days; ciprofloxacin 7 days; trimethoprim 14 days.
dz.ipc: Remove or change catheters; avoid catheter dipsticks; prophylaxis for recurrent UTI after review; cranberry evidence weak.
dz.cause: E. coli ~80%; Klebsiella, Proteus, enterococci; S. saprophyticus in young women; Pseudomonas with catheters and instrumentation.
dz.clin: Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain. Pyelonephritis: loin pain, fever, rigors, vomiting. Older adults present with delirium.
dz.pearl: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy and before urological surgery. Proteus: struvite stones, nitrofurantoin-resistant.
trial: Nitrofurantoin for 5 days gave better clinical resolution of cystitis than single-dose fosfomycin (70% vs 58%).

dz.s: Treat only symptomatic infection; bacteriuria in a catheter is expected.
dx: Change a catheter in place over 7 days, then send urine from the new one
dz.rx: As for pyelonephritis (upper tract symptoms) or lower UTI by severity; check previous cultures.

dz.s: Fever, perineal pain, tender prostate; send urine culture.
dx: Urine culture; consider STI testing
dz.rx: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD, ofloxacin 200 mg BD or levofloxacin 500 mg OD.
dz.alt: Quinolone unsuitable: trimethoprim 200 mg BD.

dz.s: Exclude torsion. STI-related (often under 35) or enteric (older, urinary tract problems).
dx: First-void urine NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia; urine culture
dz.rx: STI likely: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 10–14 days. Enteric likely: ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days or levofloxacin 500 mg OD for 10 days.

dz.syn: gonorrhoea gonorrhea neisseria gonorrhoeae gc clap
dz.s: Culture before treatment when possible (resistance). Test of cure for all.
dx: NAAT plus culture from exposed sites
dz.rx: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose if known susceptible.
dz.alt: Refer to sexual health for allergy or resistance.
dz.ipc: Partner notification; screening of at-risk groups; 4CMenB offers partial cross-protection.
notes: Partner notification through sexual health services.
dz.cause: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci; highest rates in young adults and MSM.
dz.clin: Urethral discharge and dysuria in men; often asymptomatic in women (cervicitis, PID); pharyngeal and rectal infection silent. Ophthalmia neonatorum.
dz.pearl: Report ceftriaxone treatment failures to UKHSA. Disseminated infection: arthritis–dermatitis syndrome with tenosynovitis.
trial: Gentamicin was inferior to ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea clearance, mainly at pharyngeal and rectal sites.

dz.s: Often asymptomatic.
dx: NAAT (vulvovaginal swab or first-void urine; rectal or pharyngeal if exposed)
dz.rx: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days.
dz.alt: Pregnancy or doxycycline unsuitable: azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg OD for 2 days. LGV: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.
dz.ipc: National Chlamydia Screening Programme for under-25s; partner notification; condoms.
notes: Partner notification.
dz.cause: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D–K (genital), L1–L3 (LGV), A–C (trachoma). Obligate intracellular with elementary and reticulate bodies.
dz.clin: Mostly asymptomatic; urethritis, cervicitis, PID, epididymitis. LGV: proctitis in MSM, inguinal buboes. Sequelae: tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy.
dz.pearl: Reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis). Neonates: conjunctivitis and afebrile pneumonia — treat with a macrolide.
trial: Doxycycline cured 100% of rectal chlamydia in MSM vs 74% with azithromycin — doxycycline now first-line.

dz.s: Stage the infection; check for neurological, eye and ear involvement.
dx: Treponemal EIA, then TPPA and RPR
Lumbar puncture if neurological signs
dz.rx: Early: benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose. Use the site’s syphilis guide for late and neurosyphilis.
dz.ipc: Universal antenatal screening; partner notification; regular testing for MSM; treat pregnant women with penicillin (desensitise if allergic).
dz.cause: Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum; sexual and vertical transmission; rising in MSM.
dz.clin: Primary painless chancre; secondary rash on palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches; latent; tertiary gummas, aortitis, neurosyphilis.
dz.pearl: Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction within 24 h of first dose. Prozone effect: false-negative RPR at very high titre — dilute.
trial: Adding amoxicillin and probenecid to benzathine penicillin gave no benefit in early syphilis, with or without HIV.

dz.s: Low threshold to treat; exclude pregnancy and surgical causes.
dx: NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia; pregnancy test
dz.rx: Outpatient: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg BD and metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days.
dz.alt: Alternative: ofloxacin 400 mg BD plus metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (avoid if gonorrhoea likely).

dz.s: Frothy discharge; treat partners.
dx: NAAT
dz.rx: Metronidazole 400–500 mg BD for 7 days.

dz.s: Not sexually transmitted in the usual sense; partners do not need treatment.
dz.rx: Metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days, or metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel for 5 days.
dz.alt: Clindamycin 2% cream for 7 days.

dz.rx: Fluconazole 150 mg single oral dose, or clotrimazole 500 mg pessary.
dz.alt: Pregnancy: clotrimazole pessary (up to 7 nights); avoid oral azoles.

dz.s: Start antivirals for a first episode within 5 days of onset or while new lesions form.
dx: Lesion swab for HSV PCR
dz.rx: First episode: aciclovir 400 mg TDS or valaciclovir 500 mg BD.
dz.ipc: Condoms reduce but don’t abolish risk; suppressive therapy reduces transmission. Near term: aciclovir from 36 weeks if recurrent.
notes: Late pregnancy: discuss with obstetrics and sexual health.
dz.cause: HSV-2 and increasingly HSV-1 (oral sex); latent in sacral dorsal root ganglia; asymptomatic shedding drives transmission.
dz.clin: Primary: painful multiple ulcers, dysuria, fever, inguinal lymphadenopathy, urinary retention, aseptic meningitis. Recurrences milder and shorter.
dz.pearl: Primary infection in the third trimester → caesarean section; neonatal HSV mortality is high even with treatment.
trial: Daily valaciclovir suppression in the infected partner halved HSV-2 transmission in discordant couples.

dz.syn: hiv new diagnosis pepse pep post exposure prophylaxis
dz.s: New diagnosis: refer the same week to HIV services; look for opportunistic infections if CD4 low.
dx: HIV antigen/antibody test (4th generation); confirm
CD4 count, viral load, resistance test
dz.rx: Antiretrovirals via the HIV team. PEP after exposure: start as soon as possible, within 72 hours.
dz.ipc: PEP within 72 h (ideally 24 h) for 28 days; PrEP for high-risk groups; universal antenatal screening; U=U.
dz.cause: HIV-1 (groups M, N, O, P) and HIV-2 (West Africa, slower progression); retrovirus targeting CD4 via CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptors.
dz.clin: Seroconversion illness 2–6 weeks after exposure: fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy. Untreated: opportunistic infections and malignancy as CD4 falls.
dz.pearl: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 <200. Delay ART in cryptococcal and TB meningitis to reduce IRIS.
trial: Immediate ART at CD4 >500 reduced serious AIDS and non-AIDS events by 57% — ART for everyone.

dz.s: Adults, pregnant women and the immunosuppressed get more severe disease (pneumonitis).
dx: Vesicle swab for VZV PCR
Chest X-ray if breathless
dz.rx: Adults presenting within 24 hours of rash: aciclovir 800 mg five times a day for 7 days. Pregnant, immunosuppressed or pneumonitis: urgent specialist advice; IV aciclovir if severe.
dz.ipc: Airborne and contact precautions until all lesions crusted.
notes: Post-exposure for susceptible high-risk contacts (pregnant, immunosuppressed): oral aciclovir or valaciclovir from day 7 to 14 after exposure (UKHSA).

dz.s: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis, then rash. Very infectious; notifiable on suspicion.
dx: Oral fluid or throat swab for measles PCR; IgM
dz.rx: Supportive. Watch for pneumonia and encephalitis.
dz.ipc: Airborne precautions (negative-pressure room) from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset. Notify on suspicion.
notes: Exposed contacts: MMR within 72 hours, or human normal immunoglobulin within 6 days for pregnant, immunosuppressed and infant contacts (UKHSA).

dz.s: Parotid swelling; complications include orchitis, meningitis and pancreatitis.
dx: Oral fluid or buccal swab for mumps PCR
dz.rx: Supportive.
dz.ipc: Notifiable. Exclude for 5 days after onset of swelling; droplet precautions.

dz.n: Scarlet fever and invasive group A strep
dz.syn: scarlet fever igas invasive group a strep streptococcus pyogenes gas
dz.s: Sandpaper rash with sore throat. Invasive disease (iGAS) is notifiable and needs contact assessment.
dx: Throat swab culture
Blood cultures if invasive disease suspected
dz.rx: Scarlet fever: phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg QDS for 10 days. iGAS: IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin (toxin), per severity.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin (scarlet fever).
dz.ipc: Exclude for 24 hours after starting antibiotics. Notifiable (scarlet fever and iGAS).
notes: Household contacts of iGAS cases may need prophylaxis (UKHSA).

dz.syn: toxic shock syndrome tss tampon staphylococcal streptococcal
dz.s: Fever, rash, shock and multi-organ failure from staphylococcal or streptococcal toxins.
dx: Remove tampons or other foreign bodies; look for a focus
Blood cultures, swabs
dz.rx: IV clindamycin 1.2 g QDS (stops toxin production; above the licensed dose, per local protocol) plus flucloxacillin (staphylococcal) or benzylpenicillin (streptococcal), or broad cover until known; add MRSA cover if risk.
dz.ipc: Streptococcal TSS: notifiable as iGAS.
notes: Consider IV immunoglobulin.
dz.cause: S. aureus TSST-1 or enterotoxins (tampons, wounds, nasal packing); S. pyogenes superantigens SpeA/SpeC (invasive infection).
dz.clin: Fever, diffuse erythroderma with desquamation of palms and soles at 1–2 weeks, hypotension, ≥3 organ systems involved.
dz.pearl: Superantigens bridge MHC class II and TCR Vβ outside the groove — up to 20% of T cells activated.
trial: In a small RCT of IVIG in streptococcal TSS, mortality was 10% vs 36% — underpowered and stopped early.

dz.syn: glandular fever ebv epstein barr infectious mononucleosis monospot
dz.s: Fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes.
dx: Monospot or EBV serology (VCA IgM)
dz.rx: Supportive. Avoid amoxicillin (rash).
dz.ipc: Avoid contact sports for at least 3–4 weeks (spleen rupture).

dz.s: Rash or lesions (often anogenital), with fever and lymphadenopathy.
dx: Lesion swab for mpox PCR (tell the laboratory)
Sexual health screen
dz.rx: Supportive. Tecovirimat for severe disease or high risk, via national guidance.
dz.ipc: Isolate; check UKHSA for the current infection-control status of each clade. Notifiable.
notes: Vaccine (MVA-BN) for contacts, ideally within 4 days of exposure.

dz.syn: tetanus wound tetanus prone immunoglobulin htig
dz.s: Assess the wound and the patient’s vaccination history.
dz.rx: Clean the wound. Give a tetanus vaccine dose and, for high-risk wounds in people not fully vaccinated, human tetanus immunoglobulin, as set out in the Green Book.
notes: Tetanus disease: ICU, immunoglobulin, metronidazole and wound debridement.

dz.s: Any fever after travel to a malarious area is malaria until 3 negative tests.
dx: Thick and thin films (×3) and rapid antigen test
dz.rx: Use the site’s malaria guide (artesunate for severe falciparum).
dz.ipc: Notifiable.
dz.cause: Plasmodium falciparum via female Anopheles; sub-Saharan Africa; VFR travellers highest risk. Incubation ≥7 days, usually within 3 months.
dz.clin: Fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, diarrhoea. Severe: impaired consciousness, seizures, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, AKI, ARDS, Hb <80, parasitaemia ≥2%.
dz.pearl: Delayed haemolysis after artesunate — check FBC at 2–4 weeks. P. vivax/ovale hypnozoites: primaquine after G6PD.
trial: Artesunate reduced mortality vs quinine in severe malaria by ~35% in Asian adults and ~22% in African children.

dz.s: Fever within 14 days of return from tropics, headache, myalgia, rash, low platelets.
dx: Dengue NS1 antigen or PCR in the first week; IgM after
FBC daily (haematocrit, platelets)
dz.rx: Supportive: fluids; paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.
dz.ipc: Warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rising haematocrit with falling platelets) need admission. Not spread person to person.
dz.cause: Dengue virus serotypes 1–4 (flavivirus) via Aedes aegypti (day-biting); South and South-East Asia, Latin America. Incubation 4–10 days.
dz.clin: Fever, retro-orbital headache, myalgia, rash, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia. Critical phase at defervescence: plasma leak, shock, haemorrhage.
dz.pearl: Secondary infection with a different serotype raises severe dengue risk via antibody-dependent enhancement.
trial: CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia) increased severe dengue in seronegative recipients — vaccinate only the previously infected.

dz.s: Erythema migrans is diagnosed clinically without testing.
dx: Without erythema migrans: ELISA, then immunoblot if positive (repeat in 4–6 weeks if negative and still suspected)
dz.rx: Erythema migrans or non-focal: doxycycline 100 mg BD (or 200 mg OD) for 21 days. Cranial nerve, peripheral nerve or Lyme carditis: doxycycline 21 days (or ceftriaxone). Central nervous system: ceftriaxone 2 g BD or 4 g OD for 21 days.
dz.alt: Doxycycline unsuitable: amoxicillin 1 g TDS for 21 days, or azithromycin 500 mg OD for 17 days (erythema migrans).
dz.ipc: Tick checks and prompt removal; long clothing and repellent. No UK vaccine.
dz.cause: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (B. garinii, B. afzelii in Europe) via Ixodes ticks; New Forest, Scottish Highlands.
dz.clin: Erythema migrans 3–30 days after bite. Disseminated: facial palsy, radiculitis, meningitis, heart block, arthritis; acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans.
dz.pearl: The same ticks transmit tick-borne encephalitis and anaplasmosis. ‘Chronic Lyme’ lacks evidence of persistent infection.
trial: Prolonged IV and oral antibiotics did not improve persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease.

dz.s: Freshwater or rat exposure; fever, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice and kidney injury.
dx: Leptospira PCR (blood early, urine later) and serology
dz.rx: Mild: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days. Severe: IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone.
dz.ipc: Protective clothing for occupational exposure; doxycycline prophylaxis for short high-risk exposures; rodent control.
dz.cause: Leptospira interrogans; rat (and cattle) urine via water, sewage and farms; watersports, triathlons, travel to flooded tropics.
dz.clin: Biphasic: abrupt fever, myalgia (calf), conjunctival suffusion; then Weil’s disease — jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage, pulmonary haemorrhage.
dz.pearl: Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction possible. Conjunctival suffusion without pus is a classic clue.
trial: IV penicillin shortened fever and renal dysfunction even when started late in severe leptospirosis.

dz.s: Unpasteurised dairy or animal exposure; fever, sweats, spondylitis.
dx: Blood cultures (warn the laboratory: hazard group 3)
Brucella serology
dz.rx: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 6 weeks plus gentamicin for the first 7 days (or rifampicin for 6 weeks).
dz.ipc: Notifiable.

dz.s: Farm animal exposure; flu-like illness, pneumonia or hepatitis; endocarditis later.
dx: Coxiella serology (phase I and II antibodies)
dz.rx: Acute: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days. Endocarditis: doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for at least 18 months (specialist).

dz.s: Freshwater exposure in Africa; often asymptomatic, eosinophilia.
dx: Serology at least 6–12 weeks after last exposure; urine or stool microscopy
dz.rx: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg (single dose or two divided doses), repeated after 6–12 weeks in many protocols.
notes: Acute (Katayama) syndrome: specialist advice; steroids may be needed.

dz.s: Lifelong infection that can become fatal hyperinfection on steroids.
dx: Serology; screen before steroids or immunosuppression if from an endemic area
dz.rx: Ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg OD for 2 days (repeat after 2 weeks in some protocols).

dz.syn: vhf viral haemorrhagic fever ebola lassa marburg cchf
dz.s: Fever within 21 days of return from an affected area. High-consequence infection.
dx: Use the UKHSA VHF risk assessment algorithm before any tests
dz.rx: Isolate and discuss with the infection specialist on call and the Imported Fever Service.
dz.ipc: High-consequence infectious disease: strict isolation; notifiable.

dz.syn: tb tuberculosis mycobacterium tuberculosis latent ltbi
dz.s: Notifiable. Multidisciplinary TB team.
dx: Sputum ×3 for smear, culture and rapid molecular test (resistance)
Chest X-ray, HIV test
dz.rx: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months. Use the site’s TB guide for doses.
dz.ipc: Notifiable. Airborne precautions for suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
dz.cause: M. tuberculosis complex; airborne droplet nuclei. Risk: birth in high-incidence country, HIV, homelessness, prison, anti-TNF therapy, diabetes.
dz.clin: Cough >3 weeks, haemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss; upper-lobe cavitation. Extrapulmonary: nodes, spine (Pott’s), meninges, miliary.
dz.pearl: Rifampicin induces CYP450 — OCP, warfarin and antiretrovirals fail. Ethambutol: optic neuritis; isoniazid: neuropathy, hepatitis.
trial: A 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen was non-inferior to the standard 6-month regimen for drug-susceptible TB.

dz.s: Pregnancy, older age, immunosuppression; bacteraemia and meningitis.
dx: Blood cultures, CSF
dz.rx: Amoxicillin 2 g every 4 hours IV, with or without gentamicin. Cephalosporins do not work.
dz.alt: Penicillin allergy: co-trimoxazole.

dz.syn: rabies bat bite dog bite abroad
dz.s: Any bat contact, or a mammal bite or scratch abroad.
dz.rx: Wash the wound for 15 minutes. Risk-assess with UKHSA; vaccine with or without immunoglobulin as advised.

dz.s: An emergency: antibiotics within an hour.
dx: Blood cultures (line and peripheral)
dz.rx: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g QDS IV per local policy.
dz.ipc: Quinolone prophylaxis in some high-risk haematology patients; G-CSF; neutropenic diet and line care; posaconazole in AML induction.
dz.cause: Gram-negatives including P. aeruginosa; CoNS and S. aureus from lines; viridans strep with mucositis; Candida and moulds if prolonged.
dz.clin: Often fever alone — inflammation is blunted. Assess lines, mucosa, perianal region, lungs; septic shock can develop rapidly.
dz.pearl: Door-to-needle under an hour. MASCC ≥21 identifies low-risk patients suitable for oral co-amoxiclav plus ciprofloxacin.
trial: Stopping empirical antibiotics after 72 h apyrexia and recovery, regardless of neutrophil count, was safe.

dz.s: Breathlessness, hypoxia on exertion; HIV with low CD4, steroids, transplant.
dx: Induced sputum or BAL for Pneumocystis PCR
Serum β-D-glucan
dz.rx: Co-trimoxazole 120 mg/kg/day IV or orally in 3–4 divided doses (lower doses also used). HIV with pO₂ under 9.3 kPa: add prednisolone.
dz.alt: Alternatives: clindamycin plus primaquine (check G6PD), or atovaquone for mild disease.
dz.dur: 21 days in HIV; usually 14–21 days otherwise.
dz.ipc: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 <200 or after transplant; separate PCP patients from other immunocompromised hosts (airborne clusters).
dz.cause: Pneumocystis jirovecii, a fungus without ergosterol. HIV with CD4 <200, transplant, high-dose steroids, chemotherapy.
dz.clin: Insidious dyspnoea, dry cough, exertional desaturation; CXR bilateral perihilar ground-glass or normal. Pneumothorax risk.
dz.pearl: Echinocandins and azoles are inactive — no ergosterol target. Check G6PD before primaquine or dapsone.
trial: Adjunctive corticosteroids reduced death and respiratory failure in HIV-associated PCP with hypoxaemia.

dz.s: Never a contaminant.
dx: Repeat blood cultures until negative
Eye examination, echo if persistent
dz.rx: An echinocandin first; step down to fluconazole if susceptible and stable.
dz.dur: 14 days after the first negative culture.
dz.ipc: Echocardiography and fundoscopy in all candidaemia; C. auris: single room, contact precautions, admission screening (groin, axilla, nose).
dz.cause: C. albicans; C. glabrata (reduced fluconazole, older adults); C. parapsilosis (lines, neonates); C. krusei (intrinsic fluconazole resistance); C. auris.
dz.clin: Fever in ICU patients with CVCs, TPN, abdominal surgery, broad-spectrum antibiotics; endophthalmitis, endocarditis, hepatosplenic disease.
dz.pearl: C. auris is misidentified by older biochemical systems; persists on surfaces — use chlorine or hydrogen peroxide.
trial: Anidulafungin outperformed fluconazole in candidaemia, establishing echinocandins as first-line therapy.

dx: CT chest; galactomannan (serum, BAL)
dz.rx: Voriconazole or isavuconazole (TDM for voriconazole).
dz.ipc: HEPA-filtered rooms for HSCT; posaconazole prophylaxis in AML and GVHD; protect patients during building works.
dz.cause: Aspergillus fumigatus, inhaled conidia. Prolonged neutropenia, HSCT and GVHD, high-dose steroids; increasingly post-influenza and COVID-19 ICU.
dz.clin: Fever unresponsive to antibiotics, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis; CT nodules with halo sign, later air-crescent sign.
dz.pearl: TR34/L98H azole resistance from agricultural fungicides. Mucorales: ribbon-like hyphae, amphotericin not voriconazole.
trial: Voriconazole beat amphotericin B deoxycholate for response and survival — it became first-line for invasive aspergillosis.

dx: Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen; opening pressure
dz.rx: Use the site’s cryptococcus guide.

dz.syn: mrsa decolonisation decolonization carriage screening mupirocin
dz.s: Decolonise before surgery and when colonised in high-risk areas.
dx: Nose, groin and other site screens per local policy
dz.rx: Mupirocin 2% nasal ointment TDS for 5 days, plus chlorhexidine 4% (or octenidine) body wash OD for 5 days.
dz.ipc: Contact precautions per local policy.

dz.syn: cpe carbapenemase producing enterobacterales cre kpc ndm oxa-48
dz.s: Carriers are not treated; infection is treated by enzyme type.
dx: Rectal swab screening for at-risk admissions
dz.rx: Treat infection only, guided by the enzyme (see β-lactamases page).
dz.ipc: Single room with contact precautions; flag the record.
